speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head N of the Estimates be reduced by $100." Last week, I spoke during the main debate on the threat of the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) and, at that time, it had just about started emerging in other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has had a relatively well-managed situation, with the majority of our cases making recovery and no fatalities to date, though, of course, this may still happen as we still have a few people in intensive care.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Worldwide though, COVID-19 is now spreading like wildfire.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Japan, the prefecture of Hokkaido has declared a state of emergency following an identification of at least 63 cases and two deaths.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The United States (US), which only recently reported its first cases, has now also had its first death from COVID-19 in Washington state, and there are fears that there may be a larger number of undetected cases, who may, in turn, unwittingly spread the disease.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Closer to home, our Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) neighbours are also dealing with the COVID-19 threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thailand has reported its first death and there are 42 cases recorded.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There was an earlier one in the Philippines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I was corrected – Indonesia has two cases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While there are many things that divide us, dealing with the COVID-19 threat may be one way for all of us to come together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And Bloomberg has recently described Singapore's response as the litmus test for dealing with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may be an opportunity for us to render help and expertise to other countries when dealing with this threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister share whether Singapore is working with ASEAN and the international community to deal with the COVID-19 threat?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, the current COVID-19 outbreak is a global concern that has widespread public health and economic implications.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As an open economy and international trade hub, Singapore is experiencing a significant impact from the outbreak.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We also have many Singaporeans living and working overseas who have been affected.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How has the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) been mobilised to support Singapore's interagency efforts to combat COVID-19?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry share with us how it had managed during the various evacuation efforts and the challenges it faced?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What lessons have we learnt from this experience?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does MFA see a need to increase our ground presence in more territories overseas so as to provide better support for Singaporeans living and working there?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does MFA foresee that it would have to initiate similar evacuation exercises in other countries should the outbreak worsen and spread to more countries?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, several bilateral issues with Malaysia took a turn at the end of 2018, such as on the maritime and airspace fronts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: While a number of these issues appear to have made progress, other issues still require discussions from both sides.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: This includes key connectivity projects, such as the Singapore-Johor Bahru Rapid Transit System Link and the Singapore-Kuala Lumpur High Speed Rail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: These are projects that will benefit both our peoples and that I hope will proceed on track expeditiously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: It is also notable that our Health Ministries have quickly set up a Joint Working Group to collaborate on tackling the COVID-19 situation across our borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: The political situation in Malaysia has evolved rapidly in recent days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: As Malaysia's closest neighbour, we have a long-term vested interest in Malaysia’s stability and prosperity, as any developments there will inevitably impact Singapore in many ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I filed this cut amongst other reasons, in view of the comments made over the course of the last year both in Singapore and Malaysia about pollution and water security issues surrounding the abstraction of raw water in Johor, an issue that affects not just Singapore but Malaysia, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, Singaporeans and Malaysians would also recall the shutting down of schools in Malaysia arising from pollution in Sungei Kim Kim in Johor last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Questions have also been raised in this Parliament about the safety of water supply and air quality, questions which would be far more immediate and pressing for our friends in Malaysia and specifically Johor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, the issue of the price of water sold to Singapore has also come to the fore strongly over the course of the year with the matter discussed on Malaysian talk shows and, unsurprisingly, in the Malaysian parliament, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so since various Malaysian states already charge more for raw water to their own fellow Malaysians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in September last year, Water Watch Penang raised concerns about the neighbouring state of Perak offering to sell its treated water to Penang at 70 sen per 1,000 litres.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The matter is coming to a head because Penang draws water from Sungei Muda, a river shared with the state of Kedah and it is estimated that the river can only cater to Penang's demand until 2025.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has a lot of experience in water collection, treatment, supply and, separately, waste management, including the discharge of effluents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The rising water security issues in Malaysia provide an opportunity to consider how both Singapore and Malaysia can look to reduce the prospect of our water agreement as a potential source of strain in our relationship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For Singapore, water from Malaysia is cheaper to treat than desalinated water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there scope for greater cooperation between Singapore and Malaysia in this regard?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, Indonesia is the most populous country in ASEAN and the largest economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Ever since the formation of ASEAN, we have had strong relations with Indonesia at all levels, from government-to-government, between the defence forces and at the people-to-people level.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In October last year, Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong mentioned at a press conference at the Istana that Singapore’s relations with Indonesia are in "good shape" and there is an "excellent relationship of trust and cooperation" built with President Joko Widodo, which has meant that both sides have prospered during the latter’s term in office.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This was said during Mr Widodo’s two-day visit to Singapore for the Singapore-Indonesia Leader’s Retreat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: At the people-to-people level, I also agree that relations are good and strong and, over the last two decades of my working life, I have dealt with many Indonesian clients and cases and with many investments by Singapore companies in Indonesia as well as Indonesians making investments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, there were a number of outstanding bilateral issues that have made the news over the last year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This has included differences between us in the administration of the regional air space, particularly the Riau Islands Flight Information Region (FIR) as well as military training.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What is Singapore’s approach to some of these outstanding bilateral issues with Indonesia, such as the management of airspace and military training?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indonesia is a key player in our region and an important partner for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are certainly one of the largest foreign investors in the country.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister update us on the overall state of bilateral relations with Indonesia, and how Singapore is engaging the second Jokowi Administration as well as the regions beyond Jakarta?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Prime Minister Joko Widodo has said that he is ready for more cooperation with Singapore, including in human development, tourism and industry.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: By the end of Mr Jokowi’s second term in 2024, Indonesia is targeted to have a growth of 6%.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But it is not just about the numbers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore needs to see beyond economic ties and see how we can forge a common future with our neighbours in the region.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What can we do, and how can we better prepare ourselves for this deeper engagement?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, Brunei and Singapore are the two smallest nations by geographical size in the ASEAN region.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Due to many similarities, we have built up a special relationship over the years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since our early days of nation-building, positive interactions between the two countries at every level, up to the highest echelons of leadership, have paved the way for many areas of cooperation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Every year, we continue to have a steady stream of high-level visits to and from Brunei.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These help to maintain the deep personal and institutional ties between the two nations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As one of Brunei's largest trading partners, there is room for further collaboration between our private sector and Brunei.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is particularly so as Brunei is in the process of diversifying its economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Ministry share an update on the progress in these areas of interest?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Against the background of increasing geopolitical uncertainty and various regional and global challenges, what areas of cooperation are we exploring to strengthen our special relationship and bring mutual benefits to our people?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore and the US established official diplomatic ties in 1966.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Since then, we have enjoyed deep and long-standing relations.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: More importantly, the relationship has been based on substantive cooperation across many areas, particularly in the economic and defence/security sectors.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The US is Singapore’s largest source of foreign direct investment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Conversely, Singapore is the US' fourth-largest Asian investor after Japan, China and the Republic of Korea.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The Prime Minister just met President Donald Trump in September last year.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is their fourth meeting since Mr Trump took office three years ago.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Twenty-nineteen also marked a key milestone in our defence relationship.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Given our mature and multifaceted links with the US, how has MFA sought to deepen cooperation between Singapore and the US?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The US today has been quite different since three years ago, with a current President who is very different from his predecessors.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Its role in the global landscape is also changing with very different dynamics.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I hope MFA could enlighten the House on how Singapore has been responding, and the way forward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, Singapore has had long-standing relationships with both the US and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These are now the two largest economies in the world and the two biggest powers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The US has been a good friend since our Independence, playing a key role in our defence relations and bringing security to the region, along with investment and trade.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In relation to China, Singapore started investing heavily in China long before China reintegrated into the world economy, and places like Suzhou Industrial Park are a testament to the long-standing and deep ties and cooperation between our countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: While our relations with both great powers are good, US-China relations have been difficult in recent times.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: There has been rivalry on multiple fronts, including over the South China Sea, the trade war that has started with the imposition of tariffs against each other and even the challenge over the fifth-generation (5G) network, with Huawei being blocked from the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore has traditionally sought to maintain good relations with the US and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: How can Singapore balance relations with the two major powers against this backdrop of intensifying rivalry?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, being part of a multinational organisation, such as ASEAN, certainly makes sense for Singapore in 1967 when, as a small nation, we could leverage being part of a larger grouping to make our voice heard and our concerns known on the world stage.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Cooperation and collaboration with our closest neighbours were also something that was and continues to be beneficial for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: However, given that things have moved on since then and given the differing rates of economic and social development within the group, I would like to ask the Minister to what extent ASEAN continues to be strategically important to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: In particular, could the Minister elaborate as to some key initiatives which keep ASEAN relevant to today's world and to Singapore as a member?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: It is also well-known that ASEAN operates on the basis of decision-making by consensus.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: While this has its benefits in that the bloc will be bound by any decision it makes, this can also come at a cost to the progress on matters which may be considered by some to be more controversial.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Would the Minister clarify if this policy is something that can or will be looked into to make ASEAN more nimble, more able to adapt and to address matters of concern more expeditiously?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Amidst the climate of major power rivalry and weakening multilateralism, ASEAN continues to be an effective driver for multilateralism which has underpinned the prosperity and peace in our region.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And for Singapore and our trading partners, ASEAN is an important source of economic potential.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How can Singapore best tap onto the opportunities afforded by ASEAN?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, over the last 50 years, ASEAN has provided an excellent platform for its member countries to cooperate to achieve political stability and economic growth in the region.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many dialogues and exchanges have resulted in strong and friendly bilateral and multilateral relations among its member countries.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, free trade agreements (FTAs) have facilitated economic cooperation and growth in various countries.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These efforts have benefited and improved the quality of life for people in ASEAN member countries through the benefits yielded through economic interdependence.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a financial and business hub, Singapore can consider hosting more ASEAN trade exhibitions and conferences.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These can be Chief Executive Officer (CEO) networking sessions, business development opportunities, sharing and skills training for future growth industries.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These business interaction opportunities can be expanded to the Asia-Pacific region.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.45 pm until 4.05 pm.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Chairman, Sir, the pace of change had taken on speed like no other in the past decade and even more so in recent years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is not only a result of globalisation but also technological disruptions, adaptability to changes and dynamics in geopolitical situations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The world today is interconnected in many ways.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Despite the intense connectivity among countries on many fronts, there are signs of bifurcation and turbulence constantly seen globally.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Amidst growing uncertainties in our region, it is important that we keep our engagement with key regional and strategic partners outside our immediate neighbourhood and forge closer links with countries that share similar strategic perspective as us and will offer economic and other opportunities for cooperation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As Singapore continues to be heavily dependent on trade and partnerships, we need to renew our efforts in maintaining relationships and explore new areas of cooperation with different countries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For instance, Singapore shares close people-to-people ties and multifaceted cooperation with Japan and the Republic of Korea.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With Australia, we also share similar views on the importance of an open rules-based and inclusive multilateral system.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Further, there are opportunities for cooperation with India, which is also a growing market in Asia with tremendous economic potential and promising democratic dividends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two years ago, I was at the Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh and listened to horrific stories of women being raped and how they watched their babies get stabbed to death.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I held the hand of a little girl who was shot and she showed me her bullet wound.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A young man showed me a video of the dead bodies of his entire family of seven.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two years later, all these are still fresh in my mind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What I have heard has scarred me for life and made me question my faith in humanity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But more than anything, it has scarred the Rohingyas for life and they desperately need help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat said, "As the world builds walls, Singapore must go against the tide and build bridges".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They need a way out of the huge wall built around them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand there is a need for an independent assessment of the situation in Rakhine state by the Rohingyas themselves before they will consider any repatriation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope ASEAN can help facilitate this and Singapore can ensure it is discussed at ASEAN meetings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also willing to volunteer to help with any onsite assessments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One human family connected in ways we sometimes forget".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, Malaysia and Singapore are close neighbours bound by geographical, historical, cultural and family ties.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have always been highly interdependent and our Government agencies, business entities and people have maintained their close connections through economic cycles and changes in both regional and global politics.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is substantial trade and co-investments between our two countries.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on areas of cooperation and the progress of projects we are pursuing together?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are some of the challenges that we face?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What efforts are we making to expand and deepen our engagement with Malaysia, such as building ties with the various Malaysian states?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, with the global pivot to Asia, it is more important than ever for Singapore to deepen her relationship with ASEAN countries beyond the immediate neighbours.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While ASEAN nations share core values, we are quite different in terms of our political backgrounds, population profiles, cultures and geography.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, we are highly interlinked in many areas, including trade, economic and military cooperation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also work together to overcome common environmental and security challenges.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am confident they will be well-prepared to carry on our work to promote inter-governmental and private sector cooperation within ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share an update on recent work and future plans to deepen our relationship with ASEAN countries?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, as we all know, the world is becoming even more interconnected through information and communications technology (ICT), especially when 5G technology is embraced and the use Internet of Things (IoT) devices becomes de rigour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Many hon Members of Parliament have cautioned against the corresponding risk of catastrophe occurring in the event the computer systems, particularly those that control critical information infrastructure, such as power, water and transportation networks, are hijacked by states, terrorist groups or criminal organisations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have already seen examples of such situations occurring.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The effects of such sabotage may be felt globally, too, given that a significant part of the global economy is driven by digital services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is, therefore, a clear need for the international community to come together to take steps to protect this space against such threats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean recognised this need at the Singapore International Cyber Week 2019 conference on 1 October 2019.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said as follows, "Difficult as it is, we need more dialogue and cooperation among governments and the private sector to help us to find better solutions to build a shared future, deal with sophisticated cyber threats and strengthen trust and confidence in the digital systems that we have come to depend on." I am very heartened to note that Singapore is doing its part to promote cooperation and increase preparedness within the international community and our region.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was again highlighted in Senior Minister Teo's speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, Singapore helped to organise cybersecurity exercises, such as the ASEAN Computer Emergency Response Team Incident Drill involving ASEAN countries and its Dialogue Partners.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How better prepared are we in safeguarding Singapore's cybersecurity arising from the same?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Increasingly, we are seeing the impact of climate change everywhere, through sea level rise, warmer temperatures and more frequent natural disasters.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Despite the urgent need for the international community to work together and ratchet efforts to reduce emissions, many countries have yet to fully implement the obligations or table sufficiently ambitious climate measures as called for under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Some have chosen to withdraw from the Agreement entirely.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: In view of this, I would like to ask MFA how Singapore is fulfilling its commitments under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What role can Singapore play internationally to shore up regional and global support for the Paris Agreement?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore is a member of the global coalition to defeat the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There have been a number of successful operations in recent years against ISIS and its leadership.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding, terrorism, unfortunately, continues to happen in various forms and places around the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires a strong intelligent sharing network amongst countries, particularly cooperation arrangements among frontline law enforcement and security agencies and like-minded countries forging strong alliance to fight the threat, often via multilateral and bilateral platforms.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can I ask the Minister to share on MFA's role and efforts in helping to secure Singapore from the threat of terrorism?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, in spite of political turmoil in some parts of the Middle East, Singapore has continued to maintain multilateral ties with the region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are some Singapore companies in the Middle East as well and we have always warmly welcomed visitors from the region for the purpose of medical tourism, travel and so forth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But early this year, rising tensions in the Middle East had resulted in MFA issuing a travel advisory to citizens not to remain in or travel to Iraq and Iran.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could MFA provide an update on the status of developments in the Middle East, as well as our key engagements with the countries in the region?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What other partnerships can we develop with the Middle East countries as they diversify beyond oil as an economic driver?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The government-to-government projects between the two countries offer opportunities for mutual learning and mutual benefit.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The China-Singapore Suzhou Industrial Park (CSIP) celebrated its 25th anniversary recently and is moving beyond its brick-and-mortar industrial park beginnings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With developments in professional services, intellectual property (IP) management and financial services, the CSIP has the potential to bring its successful model to third-party countries.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is also aided by the listing of China-Singapore SIP Development Group, which would provide a platform for fundraising, allowing it to finance further growth beyond Suzhou and China, and into ASEAN under the Belt and Road initiative.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The next step for the Tianjin Eco-City is to further invest into being a smart city and be a showcase for sustainable development.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Its model can then be replicated in the neighbouring areas and bring much benefit to local development.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The China-Singapore Chongqing Demonstration Initiative on Strategic Connectivity offers Singapore an opportunity to plug into China's Belt and Road initiative while also bringing benefits to the western region of China.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, recent developments arising from COVID-19 have thrown supply chains worldwide into disarray.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How is Singapore working with China to manage the impact arising from the COVID-19 outbreak so as to minimise disruptions to trade and commerce?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there specific areas for cooperation, given the existing government-to-government projects?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Technology and medical advancements can contribute towards the diagnostics, tracing and treatment of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there areas in science and technology where Singapore and China can collaborate to collectively address the threats from COVID-19?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This ranged from customs twinning to a smart city project in Shenzhen to a youth internship programme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will the outbreak of COVID-19 derail these plans?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This year marks the 30th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are new opportunities for both countries to seek together and also new challenges that need to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are our plans to commemorate the 30th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic ties between Singapore and China?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Also, can the Ministry share about new areas of bilateral cooperation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As a highly connected small city-state, Singapore is vulnerable to regional and international upheavals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And as a small state, multilateral institutions and platforms that underpin a rules-based international order are critical to ensuring a level playing field for all countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The world is going through a complex transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More countries are keen to enhance their international roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, the global consensus on the benefits of globalisation has eroded, and support for multilateralism has declined.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In many countries, nationalist, isolationist and protectionist sentiments have intensified.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These sentiments have reshaped their domestic politics and given rise to inward-looking and nativist policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The result, ultimately, is a more polarised world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In such an uncertain global climate, how much importance should our foreign policy place on multilateralism?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the people-to-people level, interactions are frequent, ties are warm and we encourage our youths to learn more about each other’s culture through exchanges and internships.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead, we expect global headwinds and uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Internally, Singapore is also preparing for our political leadership transition over the next few years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How might our bilateral relations evolve and what can we expect in the nature of our future collaborations?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How would these affect Singapore's place in the world?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Digital technology has transformed our communication modes in unprecedented ways.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Today, digital platforms have become the new "mainstream".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Many individuals are shifting to social media channels and closed-messaging apps to get real-time news and communicate with others.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: This development has traversed geographical, language, ethnic, cultural and income boundaries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Government agencies can harness the power of digital platforms to raise public awareness and understanding of their policies and gather feedback.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The immediate and borderless nature of digital platforms also present an opportunity for MFA to reach out to Singaporeans at home and abroad in a timely manner, especially in the event of major incidents and for foreign policy decisions that have impact on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: As digital platforms continue to evolve, Government agencies need to introduce new ways to share content in order to better engage and connect with Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Good communication and productive interaction will help build confidence and trust.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: For foreign policy, this is particularly the case.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Singaporeans need to have a better understanding of the macro picture, the objectives of our foreign policies, and even the constraints we face.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: These are important with the proliferation of misinformation and disinformation online.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, in today's uncertain geopolitical landscape, soft power is key for small countries like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Cultural diplomacy offers a human way for countries to see eye-to-eye and build meaningful, strategic and sustained cultural partnerships with other nations.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: As this MOU is going to expire soon, are there any plans to further it?

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This year also marks Singapore and China’s 30th anniversary of diplomatic relations.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the current evolving COVID-19 outbreak, are there any plans in the second half of 2020 to consolidate a list of arts and culture events to mark the 30 years of relationship?

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, I would like to highlight that our arts and culture groups have been flying our flag overseas proud and high.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Cultural diplomacy can help to broaden and deepen our bilateral relations with other countries at the people-to-people level.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: It makes for deeper and more direct relationships with our friends in the region.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This helps to strengthen our networks with our foreign partners, strengthen Singapore’s position as a valuable collaborative partner.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We are a small country and must allocate our resources well, yet also have an effective network of overseas Missions.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We seek to bring the voice of Singapore Arts to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chairman, Members of this House, I will start with a quiz.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Which two Ministries are asking for less money this year than last year?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Twenty-nineteen was a busy and eventful year for MFA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I wish to address three key aspects of our foreign policy today.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These are: first, looking after Singaporeans overseas; second, managing relations with our immediate neighbours; and, third, engaging major powers, specifically the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: MFA's mission is to uphold Singapore’s Independence and sovereignty and advance the interests of Singaporeans at home and especially overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Today, more Singaporeans than ever before are living, working and travelling overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This means more Singaporeans will occasionally run into trouble overseas, be it personal crises, epidemics, natural disasters or political unrest.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have personally met Singaporeans who have lost loved ones in tragic overseas incidents or been released from detention overseas and, most recently, Singaporeans returning from Wuhan, the epicentre of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: All these Singaporeans have shared with me that when the chips are down and when they are in a moment of great distress, what is most comforting is to hear that familiar Singapore-accented voice.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These Singaporeans are so grateful to the Foreign Service officers who go beyond the call of duty to reach out to fellow Singaporeans at the point in need.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They know we will leave no Singaporean behind.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is a 24/7 commitment, and I do want to express our deepest appreciation to all our consular officers all over the world who are doing this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is telling that this year's MFA debate began with questions from Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Joan Pereira on COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: New cases are occurring daily across the globe.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singaporeans, understandably, are concerned about their well-being and their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As Prime Minister Lee highlighted in his televised address on 8 February 2020, this is also the time for Singaporeans to pull together in solidarity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: While the focus is on containing and overcoming the crisis at home, we must do our best to take care of Singaporeans abroad affected by the travel restrictions or, indeed, are at risk of exposure to the virus themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: MFA worked closely with the Ministry of Health (MOH), the Ministry of Transport (MOT), the Ministry of Home Affairs, several other agencies and with the airline Scoot to arrange the flight repatriations and quarantine measures for our returning Singaporeans, for their safety and for the larger population.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Whilst many people were trying to leave Wuhan, it is noteworthy that our pilots, flight crew, nurses and MFA consular officers volunteered to fly into the epicentre of the epidemic.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They went beyond the call of duty to bring fellow Singaporeans home.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These officers themselves had to be quarantined for 14 days, separated from their family members.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Their service, their personal sacrifice should be recognised and commended.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I believe this was a display of the Singapore spirit at its best, tested and proven in a time of crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our Embassy in Beijing had to coordinate closely with the Chinese government at the centre and with the Hubei provincial government to arrange these repatriation missions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our decision around that same time to impose travel restrictions on travellers from mainland China was not an easy one.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our paramount consideration was to protect public health in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: After all, we are a densely populated city-state and we are an international transportation hub.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We did not want to import nor export infection.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These stringent measures were necessary to prevent the virus from spreading here.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These measures, I should add, were not directed at any specific country, nationality or race, but we recognised that this could impact our bilateral relations with China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We, therefore, gave China a "heads-up" before making the public announcement and we made a special effort to explain why we had to do this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When I spoke to a senior Chinese leader recently, he conveyed China's understanding of the actions that we had taken due to the unique circumstances faced by Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think his exact words to me were, "我们可以理解你们的特殊情况".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Two weeks ago, I was in Vientiane for a Special Meeting of the ASEAN Coordinating Council (ACC) and a Special ASEAN-China Foreign Ministers Meeting.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We reaffirmed the importance of openness, decisiveness and cooperation to collectively address the crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When I stood here a year ago, I said peace and stability for our immediate neighbourhood are absolutely essential.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Well, recent events just in the last one week have underlined this imperative.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As our closest neighbours, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei will always be of special importance to us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim asked about our relationship with Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members will know that our ties with Malaysia are deeply rooted in history, the people-to-people ties and business links.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: More than 300,000 people cross our land links daily for business, work and other reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Causeway is one of the busiest cross-border road links in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both countries, Malaysia and Singapore, are each other's second-largest trading partner and also important investment partners for each other.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: More personally, many of us seated in this Chamber will have family members or relatives who are Malaysian or who live in Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We, therefore, have long-standing and broad-ranging relations with Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Over the years, we have worked with successive Malaysian governments for the mutual benefit of both countries.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, Prime Minister Lee telephoned him yesterday to convey his congratulations personally.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We look forward to Prime Minister Muhyiddin forming his new cabinet soon.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: He has not announced it yet but we know many of the personalities who are potential cabinet members and we know them from our prolonged engagement over decades and we wish them sincerely all the very best.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These are mutually beneficial projects for both countries.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But after the Pakatan Harapan government took office in May 2018, Members will recall that these projects were delayed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When that happened, Singapore could have enforced our legal rights and we could have sought full compensation from Malaysia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But in the spirit of constructive bilateral cooperation, at Malaysia's request, we agreed to temporarily suspend both projects through formal agreements and we gave Malaysia time – time to review their position and to propose amendments to what both sides had, in fact, agreed to contractually before.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: However, these major infrastructural projects cannot be suspended indefinitely.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At some point, we do need to decide whether to proceed or not.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We look forward to hearing from Malaysia on these two projects in particular in the coming months.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At the same time, we have continued to have a constructive discussion on the maritime boundary delimitation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members will recall the problems that we had last year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have been able also to advance other areas of cooperation, including Iskandar Malaysia, more recently, setting up a Joint Working Group between our Ministries of Health on COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Pritam Singh has asked for an update on the bilateral issues, in particular, on the 1962 Water Agreement (62WA).

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Malaysia cannot unilaterally revise the price of water.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Then-Prime Minister Mahathir had raised with Prime Minister Lee on several occasions his desire to revise the price of raw water sold to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Malaysia subsequently made proposals on a new price for raw water.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the spirit of bilateral cooperation, but without prejudice to our position that Malaysia has lost the right of review, we have been willing to listen to and to discuss Malaysia's proposals on the basis that there must be a balance of benefits for both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have, in fact, had some preliminary discussions over the past couple of months over two meetings with my then-Malaysian counterpart, Dato' Saifuddin Abdullah.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have also been concerned for a very long time about the yield and quality of the water from the Johor River.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Pritam Singh, in fact, referred to the recurrent episodes of pollution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Malaysians have built two major water treatment plants which are drawing water from the Johor River upstream of Singapore's PUB Johor River Waterworks.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Malaysian water treatment plants' abstraction from the Johor River, in addition to Singapore's entitlement of 250 million gallons per day, has caused the total abstraction to exceed the Johor River's sustainable yield.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In addition to that, there have been recurrent pollution incidents in the Johor River.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These developments have forced the PUB Johor River Waterworks to shut down temporarily on multiple occasions, and I say that with the benefit of experience from my time in the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore has raised these concerns with successive Prime Ministers of Malaysia on many occasions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Prime Minister Lee previously raised them with Datuk Seri Najib Razak and also with Tun Mahathir Mohamad.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, the 1990 Water Agreement, which is a supplement to the 1962 Water Agreement, was the result of prolonged negotiations between Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Tun Mahathir.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I believe those negotiations, in fact, began in 1982.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members may not be familiar with the additional fact, which is that Tan Sri Muhyiddin played a key role as the then-Menteri Besar of Johor.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Had Malaysia exercised the right to review the price of water in 1987 as provided for by the 1962 Water Agreement, Singapore might then have made different investment decisions to develop the Johor River, including the Linggiu Dam.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In recent years, we have made further progress.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Malaysia built a barrage along the Johor River at Kota Tinggi in order to keep seawater from intruding upstream and affecting the abstraction of water from the Johor River.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Again, Members of the House may not realise how shallow Johor River is.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The seawater from the Straits comes all the way up to Kota Tinggi.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Johor's own water needs are increasing as its economy and as its population grow.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Already from time to time, Johor's own supplies have run short and the state has had to impose water rationing and buy additional treated water from PUB.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, during periods of drought, there have been occasions when they have bought more than four times their entitlement because they needed the additional water.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Even in normal times, they buy more than three times their entitlement under the Water Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is out of goodwill and this, again, illustrates the interdependence and how these arrangements have actually been of mutual benefit to both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The steps need to be taken and taken now to protect the Johor River from pollution and to enhance the yield of the river and to manage the total amount of water being drawn from the river.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore and Malaysia could otherwise end up in a very difficult situation down the road, especially in dry weather conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And if Members believe, as I do, climate change will make the situation worse.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It would undermine the sanctity of the 1962 Water agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members will recall that the 1962 Water Agreement is guaranteed by Malaysia as part of the Separation Agreement in 1965.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this is the sacred document on which we draw our Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In order to head off such an eventuality, Singapore has been prepared to hold discussions with Malaysia on these matters related to the 1962 Water Agreement upfront without prejudice to our legal position.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are even willing to discuss the possibility of Singapore sharing the cost of pollution control measures and new schemes to increase the yield of the Johor River since this is important for both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are, therefore, negotiating with Malaysia on these issues in good faith to explore a practical, durable and mutually beneficial solution for both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is like how we have successfully resolved other bilateral issues in the past.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is what Prime Minister Lee and Tun Mahathir agreed to at the 9th Leaders' Retreat in April last year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have explained all this in some detail so that both Malaysians and Singaporeans will appreciate and we are taking a consistent, a constructive and a mutually beneficial approach to the development of water infrastructure in Johor.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both sides have benefited from these arrangements and need to continue cooperating effectively and urgently to meet the future challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But ultimately, water is but one issue out of many bilateral areas of cooperation and we must not let any single issue colour the overall positive and multifaceted relationship we should look ahead to see how we can cooperate and resolve issues for mutual benefit and for the benefit of future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We, therefore, hope that when Prime Minister Muhyiddin's cabinet is formed, we will be able to pick up where we last left off and continue our discussions on the outstanding important matters, including water.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Seah Kian Peng both asked asked about Singapore's relations with Indonesia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: With Indonesia, our deep and multifaceted relationship is rooted in the belief that cooperation is beneficial for both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We convene an annual Leaders' Retreat between our Prime Minister and the Indonesian President and these retreats involve many cabinet members on both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore remains the largest investor in Indonesia with strong economic cooperation and our security agencies maintain close and regular contacts.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: However, there are issues that arise from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This framework sets out the core principles and considerations concerning these two issues.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On the basis of this framework, discussions on these two issues are proceeding separately but concurrently.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, this will be a major round of work for our negotiators and we will update the House accordingly in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For Brunei, Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked about our bilateral relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Well, our long-standing special relationship is built on strong strategic trust at the Leaders’ level, the pillars of strong defence cooperation and the Currency Interchangeability Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members will remember that the Brunei dollar and the Singapore dollar are interchangeable.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are working together to explore new areas of cooperation, for example, agri-food cooperation and FinTech, while also continuing to deepen our ties between the younger generation of leaders on both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We continue to explore opportunities for younger Singapore leaders to engage the younger generation of Brunei leaders through platforms, such as the annual Young Leaders' programme.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If Members look beyond our immediate neighbourhood, Singapore continues to be vulnerable to the vicissitudes of a rapidly evolving and uncertain global environment in the throes of a digital revolution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng asked about the mature and multifaceted links between Singapore and the US.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Well, these links reflect the vital role that the US has played in this region for both security and economic development over many decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: A rules-based global order with free trade and free flow of investments has been a formula for peace and prosperity across the globe for more than seven decades since the end of the Second World War.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore, in particular, has been a clear beneficiary, like many other emerging economies in our region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, we continue to believe in upholding international law and a global rules-based system, even as we recognise that some of these rules will need to be updated to suit a rapidly evolving multi-polar world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Although this is a presidential election year in the US, the US continues to maintain its ties with our region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US had intended to convene an ASEAN-US Special Summit in Las Vegas next week and the Prime Minister had agreed to go.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: However, the meeting has now been postponed because of the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We look forward to resuming the interactions at a high-level when the situation improves.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US has major equities in our region, and particularly in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It bears repeating that Singapore’s largest investor – let me put it the other way – the largest investor in Singapore is the US.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Since opening up 40 years ago, 改革开放 by Deng Xiaoping, China has undergone tremendous growth and transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, it has been the biggest beneficiary of globalisation and free trade.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Minister of State Sam Tan will elaborate on our bilateral cooperation with China later.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Vikram Nair has highlighted the need for us to maintain good relations with both the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Actually, the key variable is the relationship between the US and China and that determines how the rest of us will have to arrange our affairs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members will be aware that both the US and China signed what they call a Phase One trade deal in January this year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But frankly, thornier issues between them have been left to Phase Two and we hope that both countries can continue to make progress on this front.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But more fundamentally, a trade deal, even a comprehensive trade deal, between them will not resolve all the strategic contradictions between the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Going forward, both sides must make strategic choices.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On China’s part, as China seeks to increase its influence globally, China has to decide whether it wants to be a benign superpower welcomed and respected by other countries, including the US, and projecting soft power.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If so, China must be willing to make adjustments to participate within the international rules-based system and give space to others, especially other small countries.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There should be room for all countries, big and small, to have their interests represented fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Doing so will reflect China’s enlightened and inclusive view of its own long-term interests and enhance China’s standing and influence in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: However, if China does not give sufficient attention to the interests and concerns of other countries and is not sufficiently restrained in wielding its growing strength, then it may get its way on the international stage in the short term, but in the long term, this will seed resentment and pushback.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is not in the interests of China or the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The strategic choices of the US and China will shape whether the two superpowers reach a mutual understanding and foster a stable global order where the rest of us will have peace and prosperity and fair opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Or they could end up at odds with each other and leave other countries scrambling to avoid the fallout.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This would be a big step backward for humanity, not only because every country will be less secure and less prosperous, but also because it will be a more troubled and less stable world, as mutual suspicions and anxieties build up.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It will be much harder to deal with global issues like climate change and even public health emergencies, not least the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Southeast Asia has long been a theatre of major power competition.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As I have previously stressed, we want to be friends with both the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We hope wisdom and restraint will prevail on both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We do not want to be caught in their crossfire or be seen as taking one side or the other.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both the US and China must know that although we want to have good relations with both, we do not do things at their behest.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Fifty-five years ago, our founding Foreign Minister, Mr S Rajaratnam, declared to this House that the "primary task of our foreign policy will always be to safeguard our Independence from external threats".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The sweat and toil of our predecessors have ensured we retain this Independence today, a very precious thing that we cannot take for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It means we, today, have freedom of action in both domestic and internal and international policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It means we are no one's proxy, no one's stalking horse.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It means that we are able to exercise our sovereign rights in a rules-based world order governed by international law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mr Chairman, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan spoke on Singapore's relations with our immediate neighbours and the major powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: These efforts will help Singapore make friends, gain support at international fora and enable our companies to pursue economic opportunities abroad.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They also enable us to work closely with our partners to address non-traditional threats in order to keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ASEAN continues to be a cornerstone of Singapore's foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It allows us to foster regional peace and security so that we can pursue our strategic, economic and socio-cultural priorities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Despite its diversity and member states' different stages of development, ASEAN's continued stability makes it an attractive platform for major powers to engage our region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This amplifies ASEAN's collective voice on the international stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our key concern remains the right to freedom of navigation and overflight as enshrined by UNCLOS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ASEAN's security platforms, like the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting, have also facilitated an effective and sustainable security architecture in the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ASEAN also serves as a channel to coordinate collective responses to regional crises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For example, through ASEAN's humanitarian assistance and disaster relief efforts, we are able to alleviate the situation in the Rakhine State.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Through ASEAN, we support efforts to create conducive conditions for repatriation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For instance, the ASEAN Secretariat's Ad Hoc Support Team is building infrastructure and providing equipment for reception and transit centres in the Rakhine State.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We will be ready to support future comprehensive needs assessments once repatriation commences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In the meantime, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ordered provisional measures in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As a strong proponent of international law, we hope that all parties will respect the ICJ's decision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ASEAN convened a Special ASEAN Coordinating Council Meeting back-to-back with a Special ASEAN-China Foreign Ministers' Meeting two weeks ago in Laos to look into ASEAN's collective response to COVID-19 and discuss how we can strengthen cooperation with China to address the outbreak effectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Preparations are also underway for a video conference meeting between ASEAN and the EU to exchange information and best practices on COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ASEAN's success in maintaining peace and security has given investors confidence to put money in the region and in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is up from US$42 billion in 2005.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Intra-ASEAN trade remains strong and has benefited Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We also accounted for the largest share, which is 47.1% of total trade in services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This has allowed us to position ourselves as a regional trading hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: ASEAN has also increased efforts to promote tourism in the region, such as through the ASEAN Tourism Strategic Plan and the annual ASEAN Tourism Forum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Going forward, we should continue to tap on ASEAN's potential as a burgeoning consumer market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: By 2030, ASEAN is expected to be the fourth largest economy in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We should, therefore, continue to promote regional integration and deepen intra-ASEAN trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: One important component towards this goal is the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), which we look forward to signing at the earliest opportunity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Singapore, as Country Coordinator of ASEAN-EU relations, is also leading efforts to advance an ASEAN-EU Comprehensive Air Transport Agreement and to restart the ASEAN-EU FTA negotiations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Closer to home, it remains crucial that we continue to foster closer bilateral relations with our Southeast Asian neighbours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim and Mr Seah Kian Peng asked for updates on relations with Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: (In Malay):   Relations with our neighbours are strong and continue to expand steadily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We share extensive interdependencies with our two neighbours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In this regard, it is in Singapore's interest that our neighbours succeed, as a successful Indonesia and Malaysia are good for Singapore and the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is normal for issues to crop up from time to time with our closest neighbours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: How we go about resolving our differences is key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is only by maintaining good overall bilateral relations and cooperating in areas of common interest on a win-win basis, and with mutual respect, that we are able to develop comfort and trust to discuss more complicated issues in a constructive manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Because of this, we have kept up close personal ties, with exchanges in visits at the highest levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In 2019 alone, there were over 50 Ministerial-level visits and exchanges between Malaysia and Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: These exchanges allowed us to discuss a wide range of issues, including connectivity projects like the RTS Link and the HSR.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I hope that we will be able to continue making progress on these mutually beneficial projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We should also continue to work closely with Malaysia through several bilateral platforms on other issues, such as maritime boundary delimitation, the environment, economic cooperation and public health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The key is to find ways to sustain our historically excellent ties for future generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In this regard, I believe that there are many opportunities for greater engagement and exchanges among our younger generation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This will strengthen the excellent people-to-people ties we already share.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked what steps we were taking to expand our engagement, including building ties with various Malaysian states.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Beyond our relations with the Federal government, we want to strengthen our relationship with the various states in Peninsula Malaysia and with Sabah and Sarawak.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In 2019, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan visited Johor, Kedah, Penang, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang and Terengganu.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
